name: Olga Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or parties. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at about eleven with the parcel app, picking up from the depot on the ring road and doing around forty drops on the estates behind Mill Lane. Then I break, eat something in the car, and switch to the food app for the dinner rush on the high street until ten or so. I've only been doing this seven months, since the café I worked in shut, so I still get lost on the newer streets and lose time. I like being on my own in the car with the radio, and I hate the stairs in the tower blocks when the lift's out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you like being on your own. What wears you out, apart from the stairs?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The app, honestly. The pay per drop changes and nobody tells you why, there's no person to ring, just a help page. My partner Tomas is a paramedic, so between his job and my savings we're fine, but I see lads at the petrol station who live drop to drop. I go to the couriers' union meetings once a month because somebody has to push back, even if I'm the newest one in the room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say: the problem was never the robots, it's the companies running the apps. If AI fizzles out, they'll still find a way to shave ten pence off every drop. I'd post that in the union group chat and probably get three thumbs up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me personally, it means I keep my job, which is good, because I'm not someone who likes starting over. I've got about nine months of money put by from when I lived with my gran and paid no rent. So I'm not scared, but I'm not relaxed either, because the app can still change the rules any Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. I'd keep doing parcels in the day and food at night, and keep putting two hundred a month into savings. I'd keep going to the union meetings and maybe help with the leaflets for the pay campaign. I'm not going to learn some new app or tool if I don't have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a bit of a sour taste. Relief that my car and my routes still matter. Sour because AI was never the thing squeezing us anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the pay per drop changing. In this picture, does that pressure stay the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it stays. Last spring they cut the rate for big parcels without a word and I only noticed when my week came in forty short. Hype or no hype, the company still decides what my afternoon is worth. That doesn't go away just because the robots don't come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to about the app at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dario, an older driver I have coffee with at the petrol station on Mill Lane, and the union rep. Dario's been doing this eleven years and he says every new feature is just a new way to pay less. I believe him more than I believe the app.

say: AI was never the real problem; the **delivery apps** setting our pay are.
Even with no robots, the app can still **cut rates** without asking anyone.
think: I'm glad I **keep my job**, because I really don't like starting over.
My **savings** and Tomas's wage mean I'm safe, but the app still makes me nervous.
do: Keep doing **parcels by day** and food deliveries at night, same as now.
Keep saving **two hundred a month** on top of the nine months already put by.
Help the **union branch** with leaflets for the pay campaign.
feel: Mostly **relieved** her car and routes still matter.
A little **sour**, because the apps squeeze drivers whatever happens with AI.
S0.quote: Hype or no hype, the company still decides what my afternoon is worth.
fieldNote: She sees the **app company**, not technology, as the source of pressure.
Her **strong savings** keep her steady, but unexplained rate cuts still bother her.
Prefers **no change** at all and would avoid any new tools.
Leans on **Dario** and the union rep more than on official information.

steps.text: Keep the parcel round behind Mill Lane and the evening food shifts
Put two hundred a month into the savings account
Hand out leaflets for the couriers' union pay campaign

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the apps are going to use this to squeeze us even harder. If AI is doing the planning and the customer service, there's even less of a human to complain to. I'd say it at the union meeting and I'd probably sign every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my actual job is safe for a while, because a computer can't carry a box up to a flat with no lift. But the bits around it, the routes, the ratings, the complaints, will all be decided by software even more than now. That frightens me a bit, because I already can't argue with the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stick with the driving and not chase anything new. I'd ask Tomas to help me read the new terms each time the app updates, because I won't use any AI thing to explain it. I'd keep saving and I'd put my name down as a union contact for my area. If a depot job with a proper contract came up, I'd think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like the ground is moving under the app but my feet are still on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. How much of your day is hands-on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nearly all of it is hands-on: driving, lifting, finding doors, waiting at the counter for food. The thinking part is what the app already does for me, telling me where to go. So in this picture the app gets cleverer and I just keep carrying things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union branch push for in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A rule that a real person has to look at it before anyone gets kicked off the app. Two drivers I know got deactivated last year by an automatic check and never found out why. If software is going to run even more of it, there has to be a human you can appeal to.

say: I'd say the apps will use AI to **squeeze drivers** even harder.
I'd sign every **petition** asking for a real person to handle complaints.
think: My **hands-on work** is safe for a while, because software can't climb stairs.
Everything around the driving, like **routes and ratings**, gets run by software even more.
do: Keep the **driving job** and avoid any new apps or AI tools.
Ask Tomas to read each **new set of terms** with me.
Sign up as the **union contact** for her area and watch for depot jobs.
feel: **Uneasy**, as if the ground under the app is shifting but she's still standing.
S1.quote: A computer can't carry a box up to a flat with no lift.
fieldNote: She correctly sees her day as almost all **hands-on**, so feels less exposed.
Her real fear is **losing a human** to appeal to, after two friends were deactivated.
Resists AI tools so firmly she'd ask her **partner** to read app terms instead.
Would consider a **depot job** with a contract, but wouldn't go looking hard.

steps.text: Keep driving parcels and food without using any AI helper
Volunteer as the union's area contact for drivers near Mill Lane
Sign petitions for a human review before drivers get deactivated
Keep adding to the nine months of savings each month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need the government to step in before the companies do. I'd be out at whatever march the union organised, with Tomas if he's not on shift. I'd say the people who built this owe the rest of us a living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I lose this job by 2031, maybe sooner for the food side if they get little sidewalk robots going. Two years for the AI, three more for the robots, that's five years and I'm thirty-two with no trade. My savings would cover a gap, but not a whole new life, and that's what scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first thing would be to stop spending on anything big; we were talking about a new car, and that would wait. I'd keep driving while there's still money in it and put every spare penny away. I'd go to more union meetings and push for a deal on retraining money. I know I should look at a course, but I'd probably put it off until I was forced.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. Being told about robots by 2031 feels like the café closing all over again, but this time for every café.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots for hands-on work around 2031. What happens to your parcel round then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they'd start with the easy estates, the new-builds with wide paths, and leave people like me the tower blocks for a while. So I'd keep a shrinking round of the worst drops at the worst rates. That's maybe a year or two of work after the robots arrive, not a career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you hate starting over. What would starting over look like for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something with people, I think, maybe a care job or working in a school kitchen. I'd hate the first months of not knowing anything, like when I started this and kept going to the wrong door. Tomas says I'd be good with old people, but I don't want to be pushed into it.

say: I'd say the **government** has to step in before the companies take everything.
I'd join any **union march** and say the people who built this owe us.
think: I expect to **lose this job** by 2031, maybe sooner for food deliveries.
My **savings** cover a gap but not a whole new life at thirty-two.
do: Put off buying the **new car** and save every spare penny instead.
Keep driving while the **money lasts**, taking the drops robots can't do yet.
Go to more **union meetings** to push for retraining money.
feel: A bit **sick**, like the café closing again, but for every café.
S2.quote: Being told about robots by 2031 feels like the café closing all over again, but this time for every café.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose her job** within five years and has no fallback trade.
Knows she should **retrain** but admits she'd delay until forced.
Turns to **collective action** and government first, true to her progressive views.
Care work is a **possible path** she half-accepts, partly through Tomas.

steps.text: Postpone buying a newer car and keep the old hatchback
Save every spare penny from the remaining parcel and food shifts
Push the union branch to demand a retraining fund for drivers
Hold off on choosing a course until the robots actually arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: the companies shouldn't get to pocket all of it. But with a bit more time I'd say we can actually win something, a training fund, a payout for drivers. I'd say that loudly at the union and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I still lose this job, just around 2034 instead of 2031. That's seven years, and I'd be thirty-four. Seven years is enough time that I can't pretend nothing's coming, which is almost worse for someone like me who likes to put things off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep saving for the first couple of years, no big changes. Somewhere in there I'd do the free care certificate the council runs on Tuesday evenings, if Tomas nags me enough. I'd stay active in the union and try to get a deal agreed before the robots arrive, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick than the fast one. More like a dentist appointment I know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is having five years different from having two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can do one thing at a time. With two years it's panic and grab whatever course is going; with five, I can keep earning and try a care shift now and then to see if I can stand it. I'd still drag my feet, I know myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dario if this was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dario to start planning, because he's fifty-one and it'll be harder for him than me. He'd laugh and say they've been promising robots for ten years. But I'd still tell him, and I'd tell him to come to the union meeting.

say: I'd say drivers can **win a deal**, like a training fund or a payout.
The **companies** shouldn't keep all the money robots save them.
think: I still **lose the job**, just around 2034 when I'm thirty-four.
Having **time to see it** coming is hard for someone who puts things off.
do: Keep driving and **saving** for the first two years with no big changes.
Try the council's free **care certificate** on Tuesday evenings.
Press the union for a **deal before** the robots arrive.
feel: **Anxious**, but less sick than the fast picture, like a dentist appointment coming.
S3.quote: Seven years is enough time that I can't pretend nothing's coming, which is almost worse for someone like me who likes to put things off.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her **panic into dread**: she sees it coming but delays.
A **care certificate** is the first concrete step she names, nudged by Tomas.
Worries more for **Dario**, the older driver, than for herself.
Still trusts **the union** more than any individual plan.

steps.text: Keep driving parcels and food for the next two years
Keep putting part of every week's pay into savings
Sign up for the council's free Tuesday evening care certificate
Push the union for a driver deal before 2034

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this properly, so there's no excuse for leaving drivers with nothing. I'd say it in the union and I'd vote for whoever promised a real plan. I'd be less angry online, more organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine. By 2039 I'm thirty-nine, and I probably won't be driving by then anyway. My back won't want the tower block stairs forever. So a decade feels like time to drift into something else, which suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd change nothing this year except keep saving. Over the next few years I'd try a couple of care shifts, maybe help at the union office. I'd only make the jump to something new when I was sure, maybe five or six years in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared. It's far enough off that it's like weather in another town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots around 2039. Where do you picture yourself then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably working in a care home or with the union somehow, with Tomas and maybe a kid by then. I'd want a job with a real boss and a contract, not an app. Strange to say, but the robots might push me there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of you that would welcome the change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small part, yes. If robots did the tower blocks with the broken lifts, nobody would miss climbing those stairs. I just want the people who did those stairs to get looked after.

say: Ten years is **enough time**, so drivers shouldn't be left with nothing.
I'd **vote** for whoever promised a real plan for people like us.
think: By 2039 I probably **won't be driving** anyway, because of my back.
A decade lets me **drift into** something new slowly, which suits me.
do: Keep **saving** this year and change nothing else.
Try a few **care shifts** or help at the union office over coming years.
Move to a **contracted job** only once she feels sure, five or six years in.
feel: **Uneasy** more than scared, as if it's weather in another town.
S4.quote: If robots did the tower blocks with the broken lifts, nobody would miss climbing those stairs.
fieldNote: The long timeline lets her **slow pace** fit the change, which calms her.
She even sees robots **nudging her** towards a contracted job she wants.
Political action shifts from **anger** to voting and organising.
Fairness for **other drivers** stays her core concern.

steps.text: Keep adding to savings and change nothing else this year
Wait five or six years before leaving driving for good
Try weekend shifts at a care home to test the work
Vote for candidates with a funded plan for displaced drivers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028, because it would be on me before I'd made up my mind about anything. What would help is a proper training fund paid for by the companies, with a person, not an app, who helps you pick a course. And a rule that drivers get warned and paid out when an app replaces them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who we'd blame. Everyone asks what we'll do, but nobody asks who made the choice. A delivery driver didn't choose any of this, and it's always us who are told to adapt.

headlineQuote: A delivery driver didn't choose any of this, and it's always us who are told to adapt.
portrait: Olga is a **27-year-old** delivery driver who moved to the apps seven months ago after her café closed.
She has **nine months saved** and a paramedic partner, so money isn't urgent.
She dislikes change and **never uses AI**, and admits she puts hard decisions off.
She blames **app companies**, not machines, and puts her hope in the couriers' union.
Her mood moves from **uneasy** to alarmed in the fastest picture, then eases with more time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots would reach her round before she'd chosen another path.
whatWouldHelp: A **company-funded training fund** with a real person to help choose a course.
Rules that drivers get **warned and paid out** when an app replaces them.
